*The determinant of the product of two square matrices is equal to the product of the determinants.*

Symbolically, if ![](images/34/34058a2a5d1de088feed7d9825ba218394c9a8bb880b046be7b47307cdd37ce1.svg) and ![](images/25/256531b7f0ddb14dd11a59a3019a3361f1607d3fe16fa6d530a461344de8f39e.svg) are both square matrices, then

![](images/e5/e59b47ca5462a066093945e2698404e595a92e9e70a2b8c4f8b2f30df9c9fbf1.svg)

For instance, suppose that we want to find the determinant of the matrix ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) that is defined as follows:
![](images/9a/9a705ea4bd482cdf83251288108b48ff5bc7354c9d51c1b710b9e734c8a32dea.svg)

[{:db/id 17592186120630 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121022 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will consider a few more properties of determinants. Let's start with the following important property. 

> *The determinant of the product of two square matrices is equal to the product of the determinants.*

Symbolically, if ![](images/34/34058a2a5d1de088feed7d9825ba218394c9a8bb880b046be7b47307cdd37ce1.svg) and ![](images/25/256531b7f0ddb14dd11a59a3019a3361f1607d3fe16fa6d530a461344de8f39e.svg) are both square matrices, then

![](images/e5/e59b47ca5462a066093945e2698404e595a92e9e70a2b8c4f8b2f30df9c9fbf1.svg)

For instance, suppose that we want to find the determinant of the matrix ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) that is defined as follows:
![](images/9a/9a705ea4bd482cdf83251288108b48ff5bc7354c9d51c1b710b9e734c8a32dea.svg)

To easily compute ![](images/da/dab9a65c1cba3cd9f271a1910b060e5428813107b3b54945776aab3839003d45.svg), we first compute the determinants of the two matrices and then multiply the results. Also, notice that both matrices in our product are triangular, so their determinants are given by the product of the diagonal entries:

![](images/fa/fa4214541c12b0a761fd7cb17f4efc2f6b4be2c1424094483a3c2f61ab63c0a0.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5a8abcbc-c41d-5553-8b2e-daa7256d7d34" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3009 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "425217e0-d658-532e-a440-a3ddd4b953cd" :step/math-academy-id 16227 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120631}} {:db/id 17592186120631 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119778 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119592 :question/id #uuid "c5560ec9-32d6-514d-92fa-fbd77500d943" :question/math-academy-id "e-4431"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3b022adb-2663-550f-866d-3365bb2d78c9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120449} {:db/id 17592186120450} {:db/id 17592186265916} {:db/id 17592186265918} {:db/id 17592186265920} {:db/id 17592186265921} {:db/id 17592186354635}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Determinant of a Product"} :step/id #uuid "b7196473-0bc4-579e-90dc-f9136aa28e30" :step/math-academy-id 16228 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120632}} {:db/id 17592186120632 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121023 :tutorial/content "Another useful property of determinants is that, for any invertible matrix $A,$ we have

$$
\det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)}.
$$

To understand why the above property is true, remember that $A \cdot A^{-1} = I$ for any invertible matrix $A.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot {A}^{-1} & =I \\ det(A\cdot {A}^{-1}) & =det(I) \\ det(A)\cdot det({A}^{-1}) & =1 \\ det({A}^{-1}) & =\frac{1}{det(A)}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Important:** We can only apply the formula $\det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)}$ if $A$ is invertible, meaning that $\det(A) \neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "043b8a4a-8f67-5ae8-a7ae-bbda3fa2bdbe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3010 :tutorial/title "The Determinant of an Inverse Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "c3a5d472-bd0b-516a-aa13-594c8fc6b508" :step/math-academy-id 16229 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120633}} {:db/id 17592186120633 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119779 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119593 :question/id #uuid "17487f8f-4974-5aaf-8729-6b1336ca5eaa" :question/math-academy-id "e-4432"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "164c56ea-afbb-5ce4-800a-19002695db76" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049125}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120436} {:db/id 17592186120451} {:db/id 17592186265928} {:db/id 17592186265947} {:db/id 17592186265948} {:db/id 17592186329668} {:db/id 17592186329709}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "89f23361-1b55-5691-bba9-28621e40e324" :step/math-academy-id 16230 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120634}} {:db/id 17592186120634 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121024 :tutorial/content "One final important property of the determinant is that it is **linear in each row and column**. For rows, for example, this means 

$$
\begin{aligned} & det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ {◻}_{1}+{△}_{1} & {◻}_{2}+{△}_{2} & … & {◻}_{n}+{△}_{n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}] \\  & \,\,=det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ {◻}_{1} & {◻}_{2} & … & {◻}_{n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}]+det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ {△}_{1} & {△}_{2} & … & {△}_{n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

For instance, it's easy to check that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{-2}{\overset{⏞}{det[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}} & =det[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0+3 & 4+0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{det[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{4}+{{det[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{-6}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
